stem: Employees keep emailing spreadsheets of customer account numbers to external addresses. Which control BEST detects and blocks this exfiltration path?

options.text: Network DLP inspecting outbound email for sensitive-data patterns
options.rationale: Network DLP inspects data in transit at egress (like outbound email) and can block messages containing account-number patterns.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the mail server
options.rationale: FDE protects stored data if the disk is stolen; it does nothing to stop sensitive data being emailed out.
Notification sounds have no effect on preventing data exfiltration.
Larger mailboxes do not detect or prevent sensitive data leaving via email.

stem: Staff copy sensitive files onto personal USB drives. Which control MOST directly prevents this?

options.text: Endpoint DLP that blocks copying flagged data to removable media
options.rationale: Endpoint DLP agents control data in use on the device and can block copying sensitive files to USB drives.

options.text: Network DLP at the internet gateway
options.rationale: Network DLP inspects data crossing the network, not local copies to USB on the endpoint.

options.text: A firewall rule on the perimeter
options.rationale: Perimeter firewalls filter network traffic; they cannot stop local USB copying.
Wi-Fi credentials are unrelated to blocking local removable-media copying.

stem: A company shares confidential contracts with partners but wants recipients to be unable to forward, copy, or print them, with access expiring after 30 days. Which control BEST achieves this?

options.rationale: DRM/IRM enforces persistent usage rights (no forward/copy/print, expiration) on content even after it leaves the sender's environment.
DLP prevents unauthorized movement but cannot enforce view/copy/print restrictions on a document already legitimately shared with a partner.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the sender's laptop
options.rationale: FDE protects the sender's stored data, not the usage rights of a document once shared.
Password strength does not control what recipients can do with a received document.

stem: Customer-service agents should see only the last four digits of account numbers on screen. Which control MOST directly accomplishes this?

options.rationale: Masking obscures most of a value (showing only the last four digits) so agents are not exposed to the full sensitive number.
Disabling accounts blocks the agents from working, not a masking control.
Wi-Fi encryption protects transmission, not what is displayed on screen.
Resolution has no effect on obscuring sensitive values.

stem: A payment system replaces card numbers with surrogate values that map back to the originals via a secure vault, keeping real numbers out of most systems. This technique is MOST accurately called what?

options.rationale: Tokenization substitutes a sensitive value with a token mapped to the original in a secure vault, removing real data from downstream systems.
Masking obscures values and is typically not reversible via a vault mapping; tokenization is specifically designed to be reversible through the vault.
Hashing is one-way and used for integrity/verification, not for reversible substitution mapped in a vault.
Compression reduces size; it does not substitute sensitive values with tokens.

stem: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) technology is primarily designed to do which of the following?

options.text: Detect and prevent unauthorized transfer or exposure of sensitive data
options.rationale: DLP identifies sensitive data and blocks or alerts on its unauthorized movement or exposure.
DLP is a data-protection control, not a performance tool.
Backups are a separate function; DLP prevents unauthorized data loss/leakage.
DLP has nothing to do with marketing reporting.

stem: A newly deployed DLP tool misses much sensitive data and flags harmless files. Which underlying issue is MOST likely?

options.text: Sensitive data is not accurately identified (poor classification, patterns, or fingerprinting)
options.rationale: DLP effectiveness depends on accurately identifying sensitive content; weak classification/patterns cause both false negatives and false positives.

options.text: The network is too fast for any DLP to work
options.rationale: DLP operates at network speeds routinely; identification accuracy, not speed, is the described issue.

options.text: DLP inherently cannot inspect any data
options.rationale: DLP is designed to inspect data; the problem is inaccurate identification rules, not an inability to inspect.
This does not explain the false positives/negatives and is not the root cause of poor identification.

stem: A company suspects sensitive files are scattered in unknown locations across its file shares. Which DLP capability BEST helps find them?

options.text: Storage/discovery DLP that scans data at rest in repositories
options.rationale: Discovery (data-at-rest) DLP scans repositories/file shares to locate misplaced sensitive data.
Endpoint USB controls do not scan file shares to discover where sensitive data resides.
Firewalls filter traffic; they do not discover sensitive data at rest in repositories.
Spam filtering targets unwanted email, not discovery of stored sensitive data.

stem: An organization wants to enforce data-security policy (including DLP) as users interact with sanctioned and unsanctioned cloud apps. Which control is MOST appropriate?

options.rationale: A CASB sits between users and cloud services to enforce security policies, including DLP and access controls, across cloud usage.
Printer drivers are unrelated to enforcing cloud data-security policy.
Screensavers do not enforce cloud policy.
Display hardware is irrelevant to cloud policy enforcement.

stem: An organization applies a standard set of controls to all systems, then adds or removes specific controls based on each system's data sensitivity. This approach is MOST accurately described as what?

options.text: Applying a baseline and then scoping/tailoring controls to the specific risk
options.rationale: Starting from a baseline and tailoring/scoping controls to each system's sensitivity is the standard risk-based control-selection approach.

options.text: Applying random controls with no baseline
options.rationale: Random control selection lacks the consistency a baseline provides.

options.text: Using identical controls everywhere with no tailoring
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly describes tailoring per sensitivity, which uniform controls would not do.

options.text: Removing all controls to reduce cost
options.rationale: Removing all controls abandons protection, the opposite of tailored baselines.

stem: A manager asks how DLP and DRM/IRM differ. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: DLP prevents unauthorized movement of data; DRM/IRM enforces usage rights on content after it is shared
options.rationale: DLP stops data from leaving improperly, while DRM/IRM controls what recipients can do (view/copy/print/expire) with content once shared.

options.text: They are identical technologies with different names
options.rationale: They serve distinct purposes — movement prevention vs post-share usage control.

options.text: DRM prevents data movement and DLP controls printing rights
options.rationale: This reverses their roles; DLP handles movement, DRM handles usage rights.

options.text: Both only apply to physical paper documents
options.rationale: Both are primarily digital data-security controls, not limited to paper.

stem: To catch leaks of a specific confidential document even if partially copied, which DLP technique is BEST?

options.rationale: Fingerprinting/exact data matching recognizes specific known sensitive content (even partial excerpts), improving detection accuracy over broad patterns alone.
Blocking all email is disproportionate and disrupts business; fingerprinting targets the specific content.
Disabling DLP removes protection rather than improving detection.
Font changes do not help DLP detect leaked content.

stem: A retailer tokenizes card numbers so downstream systems never store real PANs. What is the MOST significant security benefit?

options.text: Downstream systems fall out of scope for handling real card data, reducing breach impact and compliance scope
options.rationale: By keeping real card data out of most systems (only tokens present), the breach impact and PCI scope of those systems are reduced.

options.text: It makes the card numbers load faster
options.rationale: Performance is not the security benefit of tokenization.
Tokenization keeps real data out of systems; it does not make publishing card numbers safe.

options.text: It eliminates the need for any access control
options.rationale: Access controls remain necessary, especially over the token vault.

stem: Sensitive data is leaking through employees uploading files to personal cloud storage via their browsers. Which DLP capability MOST directly addresses this vector?

options.text: Network DLP (or a CASB) inspecting outbound web/cloud uploads
options.rationale: Web uploads are data in transit; network DLP or a CASB inspects and controls outbound cloud uploads to block sensitive data.
Shredding addresses paper disposal, not browser-based cloud uploads.
Backups do not prevent sensitive uploads to personal cloud storage.
Password expiry does not detect or block sensitive data uploads.

stem: Digital Rights Management (DRM) is best described as which of the following?

options.text: Controls that enforce usage rights (view/copy/print/expire) on content after distribution
options.rationale: DRM persistently enforces what recipients may do with content even after it leaves the owner's environment.

options.text: A method to speed up file downloads
options.rationale: DRM controls usage rights, not download speed.
DRM is a data-control technology, not hardware cabling.
DRM is unrelated to backup scheduling.

stem: A DLP deployment blocks so many legitimate emails (false positives) that staff seek workarounds. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Tune the DLP rules/classification to improve accuracy and reduce false positives while maintaining protection
options.rationale: Tuning detection rules and classification reduces false positives so the control protects data without driving staff to unsafe workarounds.
Disabling DLP removes protection; the fix is tuning, not abandonment.

options.text: Ignore the workarounds and change nothing
options.rationale: Ignoring workarounds lets sensitive data leak through unmonitored channels.
Blocking all email is disproportionate and harms the business.

stem: Developers need realistic-looking data in a test environment but must not handle real customer PII. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use masked/obfuscated (or synthetic) data that preserves format without exposing real values
options.rationale: Masking or synthetic data lets developers work with realistic formats while keeping real PII out of lower environments.

options.text: Copy full production PII into the test environment
options.rationale: Copying real PII into less-protected test environments greatly increases breach risk.

options.text: Give developers direct production access instead
options.rationale: Direct production access expands exposure of real data rather than protecting it.

options.text: Post the data publicly for convenience
options.rationale: Public exposure of PII is a direct breach.

stem: A security architect notes that no single data-security control stops all leakage. Which strategy MOST appropriately reflects this?

options.text: Layer complementary controls (DLP, DRM, encryption, access control) as defense in depth
options.rationale: Because each control has gaps, layering complementary data-security controls provides defense in depth against varied leakage paths.

options.text: Rely solely on DLP as a complete solution
options.rationale: DLP alone has gaps; relying on one control contradicts the stated reality.

options.text: Remove all controls since none is perfect
options.rationale: Imperfection is not a reason to remove protection; layering compensates for individual gaps.
Physical security alone does not address digital data leakage paths like email or cloud uploads.

stem: After sharing an IRM-protected document with a partner whose contract is terminated, the company wants to cut off their continued access. Which IRM capability MOST directly enables this?

options.text: Revoking the recipient's access rights so the protected document can no longer be opened
options.rationale: IRM can revoke or expire access, preventing the former partner from opening the protected document even though they still hold the file.

options.text: Emailing them a polite request to delete it
options.rationale: A request relies on voluntary compliance and does not technically cut off access.
Wi-Fi credentials do not affect a document already in the partner's possession.
Deleting the sender's copy does not revoke the recipient's access to their copy.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST relevant as a data-security control for preventing sensitive-data leakage?

options.text: The brand of coffee in the break room
options.rationale: Break-room coffee has no bearing on preventing sensitive-data leakage, making it least relevant.
DLP is a core control against data leakage.
Encryption is a fundamental data-protection control.
DRM/IRM controls usage of shared sensitive content, relevant to leakage prevention.
